title: Austrian Pine: Ancient Austrian Pines You Can Visit
meta_description: Pinus nigra shrugs off bad soil: a mushroom-shaped survivor in a Montreal cemetery, a Portland street-planter giant, a Vienna park pine unaged since 1942.
intro: Austrian pine, Pinus nigra, is a Mediterranean and Balkan species that nineteenth-century cities across two continents planted for exactly what it does best: shrug off compacted, disturbed ground that would stunt almost anything else. Montreal's specimen, just inside the gate of Notre-Dame-des-Neiges cemetery, took that tolerance sideways instead of up, spreading eighteen metres wide on a trunk barely half as tall, shaped more like a mushroom than a pine. Portland's grows out of a street planter a florist put in before the street existed, in the 1870s or 80s, and has since reached 31 metres. Vienna's stands in a small park named for the writer Marie von Ebner-Eschenbach, protected as a natural monument since 1942 with no age ever recorded, an unusually thin file for a tree the city thought worth the paperwork. None of the three needed anything resembling good soil to get old.
